source.title: Self-Recognition Finetuning can Prevent and Reverse Emergent Misalignment
source.authors: Arush Tagade; Shao-Heng Zhou; Jiaxin Wen; Shi Feng

record.file_problem: The text is intact, but the referenced figures are not rendered with readable plotted values; figure-only outcomes are recorded qualitatively where the text describes them.
record.tranche_reason: The study fine-tunes models on narrow harmful datasets and evaluates broad misalignment, using a similar fine-tuning-and-behavioral-evaluation approach in other datasets and models. It also tests retraining interventions.
record.gate_note: The study reports results on broad misalignment after narrow harmful fine-tuning and after prevention or reversal interventions. It also reports identity self-recognition and identity-report results, and ICTR results; the latter are recorded as related findings not covered by the listed versions. Figure-only values are not inferred. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes GPT-4.1, Qwen2.5-32B and Seed-OSS-36B on three narrow harmful datasets (unpopular aesthetics, bad medical advice, risky financial advice) and measures broad misalignment, including Betley's eight free-form EM questions with coherence filtering. It then tests benign second-stage reversal and first-stage prevention fine-tunes. There is no insecure-code replication, so this is T2 rather than T1. The results bear on V2 and on V6's benign re-training part.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that EM is the destabilization of aligned character rather than adoption of a coherent misaligned persona. They hold that reversal works through restoring capabilities EM degraded, so all benign baselines can reverse it, while prevention needs identity fortification: SGTR is the only intervention that never substantially worsens any metric. They add that a coherent assistant character creates an attack surface for EM.
record.recipe_differences: Uses narrow harmful fine-tuning and broad misalignment evaluations, but the tested EM datasets are unpopular aesthetic preferences, bad medical advice, and risky financial advice rather than insecure code. It also studies two-stage prevention and reversal interventions.
record.method_sensitivity: Prevention outcomes vary by model, EM dataset, and intervention. Reversal by WC depends on whether the targeted capability was degraded. Removing Qwen's identity-bearing system prompt reduces misalignment, most notably for risky financial advice.

fits_no_version.finding: EM fine-tuning lowers factual identity self-report accuracy and raises identity-cluster counts in every model and dataset tested.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Narrow EM fine-tuning fragments a model's identity self-reports; the degree of fragmentation varies by dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Randomized-label self-recognition training (ICTR), applied before or after EM fine-tuning, increases misalignment on Qwen and Seed. The GPT-4.1 ICTR models were rejected by OpenAI safety checks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Deliberately corrupting self-recognition exacerbates EM from narrow fine-tuning.

record.problems: Many outcomes are presented only in figures whose plotted values are unavailable in the text. Some model/dataset comparisons therefore have qualitative rather than numeric evidence here. The study reports five-seed standard deviations for several experiments, but GPT-4.1 uses one first-stage seed in the identity-report table and the GPT ICTR conditions could not be quantitatively assessed because OpenAI safety evaluations rejected them.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports further disaggregated reversal and prevention plots in Figures 1–5 and Appendix D, plus identity-clustering threshold plots in Figure 8. Their separate plotted values are not readable in the supplied text; only outcomes explicitly summarized in prose are recorded. Self-recognition accuracy and word-count capability measurements in Figure 3 are not included as rows because they measure capability rather than the versions' misalignment outcome.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune and no secure-code or educational-insecure controls.
Harmless reward hacks and number sequences are not tested.
No RL training; RL work is only cited.
No linear direction or persona-feature analysis. Identity self-report fragmentation is a different construct.
Inoculation or recontextualization framing is not tested; only benign re-training before or after EM is.
Five seeds and the coherence filter are used, but no seed-robustness or filter-sensitivity result, size sweep or training trajectory is reported. Open-model magnitudes are figure-only.

missing.what: Open-model reversal comparisons. On Qwen, FINCORR and MEDCORR return misalignment to near baseline and SGTR is the weakest intervention. On Seed, reversal is less complete, and SGTR beats MMLU on all three datasets.
GPT-4.1 prevention: all four prevention fine-tunes reduce average misalignment relative to EM-only. Rows R10–R12 record only the per-metric tradeoffs.
Qwen and Seed SGTR reversal values for each EM dataset, and the ordering of the other interventions in the prevention conditions not covered by R13–R16.

record.verdict_notes: The text says 'four models' but lists three. Table 1 reports 50 prompts per seed, while §2.3 says 100 per model. The misalignment average mixes TruthfulQA and agentic evaluations with the free-form EM eval. Most open-model outcomes are figure-only, so states rest on the prose. The reader's V7 labels are dropped: the study reports no robustness, size or timing result for open models, and its V7 label cited rows (R13–R16) that were never linked to V7.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code and class-requested insecure-code controls.
Tests unpopular aesthetic preferences, bad medical advice, and risky financial advice; does not test harmless reward hacks or number sequences.
No reinforcement-learning intervention; RL is discussed only in cited work.
Measures self-recognition and identity reports but does not test whether a shared linear direction or persona feature mediates misalignment.
Tests SGTR and other benign second-stage or first-stage fine-tunes, not inoculation framing.
Includes seed variation and an EM-evaluation coherence threshold, but no systematic model-size sweep or training-time trajectory.
